title: He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World With Him
coreMove: Before asking for anything, name what the other person already wants and show how your request gets them closer to it — in their words, not yours.

exampleSpecs.domain: a community theater director trying to get a sullen 16-year-old stagehand to show up for a Saturday tech rehearsal he has already blown off twice
exampleSpecs.audience: a first-time volunteer director who keeps reaching for guilt and obligation
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether the lighting cues are ready for opening night, and whether the teenager quits theater entirely after this season
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the director stops rehearsing the speech about responsibility and asks what the teenager would get out of running the board himself during the run — and builds the ask from that answer

exampleSpecs.domain: a rural large-animal veterinarian trying to convince a third-generation dairy farmer to switch his herd onto a pricier mineral supplement
exampleSpecs.audience: a vet two years out of school who keeps losing these conversations by citing research
exampleSpecs.stakes: the farmer's milk yield, a 20-year client relationship, and whether the vet's practice can keep its largest account
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the vet drops her citation mid-sentence and instead asks what the farmer noticed about his cows last winter, then frames the supplement as the answer to the thing the farmer himself just described

exampleSpecs.domain: a 74-year-old widower trying to get his 41-year-old daughter to accept weekly help with his insulin injections
exampleSpecs.audience: an aging parent who hates being a burden and has been refusing help for months
exampleSpecs.stakes: his independence, her anxiety at 2am phone calls, and the unspoken question of whether he moves in with her
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the father names out loud the thing his daughter is actually afraid of — missing the call that matters — and lets the weekly visit be the thing that protects her, not him

exampleSpecs.domain: a self-employed plumber writing a quote to a small landlord for re-piping a 1920s triplex
exampleSpecs.audience: a tradesman whose quotes keep getting undercut by bigger outfits
exampleSpecs.stakes: a $14,000 job, six weeks of steady work, and whether the landlord calls him back for the other two buildings on the block
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the second version of the quote opens with the tenant complaints the landlord mentioned on the walk-through, not with the plumber's credentials or the pipe specs

exampleSpecs.domain: a high school speech-and-debate coach reviewing why her proposal for eight refurbished laptops was turned down by the principal last spring
exampleSpecs.audience: a teacher writing the same proposal again for this year's budget cycle
exampleSpecs.stakes: the team's ability to compete in remote rounds, and the coach's standing with an administration that thinks debate is a luxury
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the coach realizes her pitch spoke entirely about what her students needed and never named the metric — graduation rates, district rankings — that the principal is judged on every June

exampleSpecs.domain: you want your next-door neighbor to prune the old plum tree that drops fruit and wasps into your toddler's sandbox every August
exampleSpecs.audience: the reader, who has rehearsed a polite but pointed note three times and not delivered it
exampleSpecs.stakes: a summer of stings, the sandbox your kid loves, and eleven more years of sharing a fence with this household
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the reader drafts the ask twice — once starting from their own grievance, once starting from something the neighbor has said they care about (the tree's history, the fruit, the quiet) — and notices which version they would answer yes to
